content: The document outlines the Zero by 30 global strategic plan, which aims to eliminate human deaths caused by dog-mediated rabies by the year 2030. This initiative is a collaborative effort led by four major organizations: the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), and the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC). These organizations have united under the United Against Rabies collaboration to address this preventable disease. Rabies, a fatal disease caused by infection with a lyssavirus, is responsible for approximately 59,000 human deaths annually, with one person dying every nine minutes. Nearly 40% of these victims are children living in Asia and Africa. The disease is primarily transmitted through dog bites, which account for 99% of human rabies cases. The plan emphasizes the importance of mass dog vaccination, which is a cost-effective method to break the transmission cycle of rabies at its source. Sustained vaccination coverage of at least 70% of the dog population is sufficient to halt the spread of the disease between dogs and from dogs to humans. This approach not only saves lives but also strengthens health systems by improving disease surveillance, expanding access to healthcare, and fostering collaboration between human and veterinary health sectors under the One Health framework. The Zero by 30 strategy is structured into three phases: 1. Start-Up Phase (2018–2020): Establishing a strong foundation by supporting 29 countries in developing sustainable national rabies elimination plans. 2. Scale-Up Phase (2021–2025): Expanding efforts to include 52 additional countries, bringing the total to 81 endemic countries engaged in rabies elimination. 3. Mop-Up Phase (2026–2030): Engaging the remaining endemic countries to achieve global elimination of dog-mediated rabies. The plan prioritizes three key objectives: 1. Effective Use of Vaccines and Tools: Increasing access to vaccines, medicines, and healthcare while improving public awareness and education about rabies prevention. 2. Data-Driven Decision-Making: 3. Sustaining Commitment and Resources: The initiative highlights the societal and economic benefits of rabies elimination, particularly for vulnerable populations in poor and rural areas. By reducing the burden of rabies, countries can improve equity in healthcare access, strengthen health systems, and contribute to sustainable development goals (SDGs), such as ending poverty and ensuring universal health coverage. The document also acknowledges the historical progress made in rabies prevention, including the development of the first human rabies vaccine by Louis Pasteur in 1885 and successful elimination efforts in regions like Western Europe, North America, Japan, and parts of Latin America. These achievements demonstrate that rabies elimination is feasible with existing tools and technologies, even in resource-limited settings. The United Against Rabies collaboration leverages the expertise and resources of its partner organizations to empower countries to take ownership of their rabies elimination programs. By fostering international cooperation and integrating rabies prevention into broader healthcare initiatives, the plan aims to achieve the shared goal of zero human deaths from dog-mediated rabies by 2030.
